cat_1.reason:
Washing this item in the dishwasher ruins its material properties.

Wood absorbs water and cracks under high heat, metals like copper and aluminum oxidize and discolor, and delicate crystal or antique finishes suffer permanent clouding or chipping due to vibrations and aggressive detergents.

cat_2.reason:
Some versions of this item are chemically formulated and treated to withstand microwave heat, while others are not.

Using an unlabeled version risks melting the material, leaching harmful plasticizers like phthalates into your food, or creating a toxic chemical hazard.

cat_3.reason:
Heating this item in the microwave is extremely dangerous.

Materials like Styrofoam melt and release toxic styrene, thin plastics leach chemicals, and paper bags or dry materials can catch fire under intense electromagnetic waves.

cat_4.reason:
Freezing this item degrades its quality or creates a safety hazard.

Eggs in shells expand and crack, emulsions like mayonnaise separate into oily layers, and glass bottles shatter due to liquid expansion.

cat_5.reason:
Putting this item in the oven will ruin the item or cause a safety risk.

Materials like untempered glass will shatter from thermal shock, wood will scorch and warp, and certain non-stick coatings release toxic fumes at high heat.

cat_6.reason:
Machine drying this item will ruin the material or damage the dryer.

Adhesives in running shoes melt, delicate fabrics like silk tear, and heavy items like backpacks can damage the dryer drum.

cat_7.reason:
Washing or placing this item in the air fryer is highly unsafe.

Materials like plastic or Styrofoam melt instantly, wet batter drips through the basket grate and burns, and dry paper items can catch fire near the heating element.

cat_8.reason:
Air fryers work by circulating extremely hot air at high velocity, causing rapid and localized temperature changes.

Most glass bowls, even those rated oven-safe, are not designed to withstand such rapid and uneven thermal expansion, leading to a high risk of the glass cracking or shattering violently.

cat_9.reason:
While the refrigerator prevents mold, the cold and dry air accelerates starch retrogradation in bread.

This causes the starch molecules to crystallize, drawing moisture out of the crumb and making the loaf go stale, dry, and tough much faster than it would at room temperature.

cat_10.reason:
Storing this item in the refrigerator ruins its flavor, texture, or causes it to crystallize.

For example, tomatoes become mealy and tasteless, honey solidifies into a gritty block, and olive oil thickens and turns cloudy, making it impossible to pour.

cat_11.reason:
The clothes dryer is designed strictly for fabrics. Placing food items, hard containers, or cookware in the dryer will create a massive mess, cause damage, and is a major fire hazard.

Keep all food, liquids, and hard objects out of the clothes dryer.

cat_12.reason:
Liquids expand by about 9% when frozen. If you freeze food in a rigid glass jar without leaving at least an inch of headspace, the pressure will shatter the glass.

Always use wide-mouth, tempered canning jars (like Mason jars) and leave headspace, or use plastic/silicone containers.

cat_13.reason:
Tempered glass (like Pyrex) is designed to handle oven temperatures. However, it is still vulnerable to thermal shock (rapid temperature changes).

Never place hot glass on a cold countertop, wet surface, or expose it to direct broiler flame.

cat_14.reason:
An air fryer operates under the same heating principles as an oven, but heats up much faster. Tempered glass containers are safe, but thin glassware will shatter from the rapid heat change.

Always use oven-safe pans or silicone inserts.

cat_15.reason:
This material is fully stable at standard refrigerator temperatures (35°F to 40°F). Storing items in the fridge does not degrade the material and is safe.

Glass, plastics, silicone, and metals are all perfectly fine.

cat_16.reason:
This material is stable at cold temperatures and does not contain water that will expand or shatter the container.

Plastics, metals, and silicone items are perfectly fine in the freezer.

cat_17.reason:
Materials like plastic, wood, paper, or styrofoam will melt, release toxic fumes, or catch fire inside the hot oven.

Only use cookware specifically labeled as oven-safe.

cat_18.reason:
Plastics, paper plates, or wood will melt, catch fire, or release toxic chemical fumes inside the high-heat, high-airflow environment of the air fryer.

Stick to oven-safe metal, glass, or silicone accessories.

cat_19.reason:
Many plastic materials have a low melting point and can warp or release harmful microplastics when exposed to the high heat of a dishwasher's drying cycle.

Always check the bottom of the item for the dishwasher-safe symbol. If safe, place it exclusively on the top rack, away from the bottom heating element.

cat_20.reason:
Plastics not rated for the microwave can melt when in contact with hot fats or sugars in food. This melting process leaches dangerous plasticizers (such as BPA or phthalates) directly into your food.

Only use containers certified by the manufacturer as microwave-safe.

cat_21.reason:
Dishwasher detergents are highly alkaline and contain abrasive particles designed to strip grease. When you put reactive materials like wood, cast iron, copper, or fine gold trim in the dishwasher, the environment destroys them.

Wood splits and warps, cast iron strips its seasoning and rusts, and gold coatings are worn away by the abrasive wash cycle.

cat_22.reason:
This material is highly heat-resistant and will not melt, warp, or release toxic chemicals at standard baking temperatures (up to 450°F or 500°F).

Stainless steel, cast iron, and food-grade silicone are excellent choices for oven cooking.

cat_23.reason:
Any cookware or container that is oven-safe (such as stainless steel, cast iron, or food-grade silicone) can be safely placed in the air fryer basket.

Ensure the pan is small enough to allow air to circulate around the sides.
